summary:
Çorum province stands under the national framework applicable across Türkiye, and that framework presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft of Türkiye's 11th Judicial Package would amend penal-code article 225 to punish conduct "contrary to biological sex" with up to three years in prison, and would allow charges against anyone taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony, carrying up to four years. Under civil-code article 40 the same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 and impose a permanent-infertility mandate, with providers facing fines and up to seven years and patients up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association objected, and Human Rights Watch called for withdrawal; the measure had not been passed when reported.

Kaos GL's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025, published 24 February 2026 under the title "A Major Siege", finds that hostility toward LGBT people became explicit state policy during 2025, driven by "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions. The report documents 313 right-to-liberty violations, roughly two and a half times the previous year's total and mostly detentions, alongside 89 torture and ill-treatment violations, up from 51, and six right-to-life violations including three hate-motivated killings, with trans people most affected. Türkiye keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so these figures rest on media monitoring rather than state records.

Enforcement already runs ahead of the pending legislation. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in streets, shops and cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release; legal experts cited in the reporting argue these checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detainee stated that no fines were issued but that the women were documented anyway, and that enforcement was being applied before any new law had been passed. Foreign nationals stopped at such checkpoints must produce original identity documents, and Turkey requires foreigners to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, every checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people is lethal and the state response asymmetric. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Trans prisoners are held according to registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025. The Prison Insider country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted healthcare access, refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners, binary and heteronormative administration with no staff training on LGBT needs, transfers that disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints mechanisms that are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued, risking the profiling of trans patients in official records and restricting access to care.

For Çorum specifically, the source inventory records no province-specific enforcement, incidents or facilities. The province is assessed against the national picture: the draft package, the detention pattern, the document-carrying requirement and the prison and healthcare rules apply here as they do elsewhere in Türkiye, and a visitor should expect checkpoint document checks and official record-keeping to behave as described above rather than as a local variant.
tangentialFactors:
The 11th Judicial Package remained a draft as of October 2025, but the reporting indicates authorities were already acting on its terms; pending status should not be read as suspension of enforcement. The Kaos GL figures are national and derived from media coverage because the state maintains no hate-crime statistics, so documented totals understate rather than overstate incidence.

Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

Çorum's interior location and distance from the coastal and metropolitan centres where most documented incidents occurred shape the risk profile: the visible flashpoints in the record are Istanbul and Ankara, while Çorum's exposure runs through the same national legal and administrative machinery rather than through a local pattern of reported events.
localsOnly:
Residents of Çorum live under the same penal-code and civil-code provisions as the rest of Türkiye, including the existing framework governing gender-affirming care and the identity-document regime administered through the civil registry. The draft 11th Judicial Package would raise the care minimum age to 25 with a permanent-infertility mandate if enacted, directly affecting residents seeking transition-related treatment.

The Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 requires e-reports and removes the "other" option from hospital records, which changes how local health directorates and hospitals document gender-related care for residents as well as visitors. Kaos GL's reporting indicates that "Year of the Family" instructions were directed at public institutions generally, so municipal and provincial bodies in Çorum operate under the same policy framing.

Detention and ill-treatment figures in the Kaos GL report are national, and the state's absence of official hate-crime statistics means residents' experiences of violence or police contact are unlikely to enter any official count.
outOfScopeNotes:
No province-specific enforcement, incidents, detention records, pride events, facilities or healthcare providers for Çorum appear in the source inventory; the province's profile is assembled from national material and remains unverified at local level.

Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been introduced, amended or enacted since the October 2025 reporting is unresolved in the sources supplied; the record captures it as a leaked draft under objection.

The current status of the Health Ministry regulation, and whether the Kayseri circular's approach has been applied by the Çorum Provincial Health Directorate, is not sourced here.

Local police practice in Çorum regarding identity-document checks of trans visitors, and any provincial detention figures, are not documented in the inventory and cannot be confirmed or excluded from it.
